title: Uhud: those who shielded him
hook: Nusaybah bint Ka'b, Talhah and Abu Talhah shield the wounded Prophet ﷺ with their bodies, and Fatimah tends his wound (sirah; Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uhud, and the archers who left their post for the spoils. Your line was: stay on the hill. Did you give something five more minutes before you called it done? Day seven hundred eighty.

Same battle, a little later. The hill is empty, the enemy has come around it, and the Muslim lines have broken. People are running. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is hurt, and a rumor goes through the field that he has been killed. Around him, a handful of people do the opposite of running. They close in. One of them came out that morning carrying nothing but a water skin. Her name was Nusaybah bint Ka'b, and she is remembered as Umm Umarah. Today: Uhud, and the ones who stood in front.
screen: `THE LINES HAVE BROKEN.` → `A HANDFUL CLOSE IN.` → `SHE CAME OUT CARRYING WATER.`

segments.voice: Nusaybah's story comes to us through the early biographers, in Ibn Ishaq's account. Later, another woman asked her what happened at Uhud, and she told it plainly. She had gone out early with a water skin, to give the fighters a drink. When the Muslims were routed, she went to where the Prophet was, and she fought, with a sword and with a bow, to keep people away from him, until she was wounded herself. The woman who asked her said she saw the scar on her shoulder, deep and hollow. Nusaybah was not the only one. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps two more. A man named Qays says he saw the hand of Talhah ibn Ubaydullah, paralyzed. It was the hand he had held up to shield the Prophet at Uhud. And Anas says that Abu Talhah stood before the Prophet with his shield, a strong archer, and when the Prophet raised his head to look at the enemy, Abu Talhah told him: don't look out, an arrow might hit you. My chest before your chest. Then there's what came after. Bukhari reports that the Prophet's face was cut, his helmet broken on his head, a tooth broken. Fatimah, his daughter, the bride from two days ago, washed the blood from his face while Ali poured water from his shield. When the bleeding wouldn't stop, she burned a piece of a reed mat and pressed the ash into the wound, and it stopped. A water skin, a raised hand, a shield, a handful of ash. Four people, four small things. Each of them stood between him and harm.
screen: `A WATER SKIN, THEN A SWORD AND A BOW.` · `TALHAH'S HAND, PARALYZED.` · `MY CHEST BEFORE YOUR CHEST.` · `FATIMAH AND THE ASH.` · then, large: `SHE STOOD IN FRONT.`

segments.voice: The practice: stand by someone under attack. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who's taking blows right now. Maybe online, maybe at work, maybe in their own family, maybe in their own head. Picture them clearly. Then picture yourself stepping a little closer, the way Nusaybah moved toward the Prophet instead of away. You don't need a sword. Ask what your water skin is, what your shield is, what your ash is: a message, a word in a meeting, a meal dropped at the door. Choose one. If you pray, you can ask Allah to protect them. If you don't, just keep them in front of you. The bell holds the time.
Uhud, again: the battle where the lines broke, and Nusaybah, Talhah, Abu Talhah and Fatimah each stood between the Prophet and harm. Today's word.
Your line: she stood in front. Today, do the one thing you chose for the person under attack, before the day is out. Day seven hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the defenders of Uhud in sirah lessons and sermons, and Nusaybah bint Ka'b, Umm Umarah, is named as an example of women's courage in the early community.

pairs: came out with water, then fought
a hand paralyzed shielding the Prophet

myth: Nusaybah went out to Uhud to fight
in her own telling, she went out with a water skin to give the fighters a drink, and fought only when the lines broke.
Talhah's hand was paralyzed from shielding the Prophet ﷺ
Qays says in Bukhari that he saw it, the hand Talhah held up at Uhud.
the Prophet's bleeding was stopped with cold water
water didn't stop it; Fatimah burned a piece of a mat and pressed the ash into the wound.

fork.setup: you've come to the battle carrying a water skin for the fighters. the lines break and people are running past you. what do you do?
options: keep handing out water at the back.
go to where the Prophet ﷺ is.
fork.reveal: in her own account, Nusaybah went to the Prophet and fought to keep people away from him, until she was wounded.

original.note: Arabic: Nusaybah, the name of Umm Umarah, who shielded the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about soldiers.
what it means: a woman with a water skin, a hand held up, a chest, and ash, each standing between him and harm.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq's interview with Umm Umarah, beside Bukhari's reports of Talhah, Abu Talhah and Fatimah.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (via Ibn Hisham): Umm Umarah, Nusaybah bint Ka'b, at Uhud, in her own telling
Sahih al-Bukhari 3724 (Qays: Talhah's hand, paralyzed from shielding the Prophet)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3811 (Anas: Abu Talhah with his shield; 'my chest before your chest')
Sahih al-Bukhari 2911 / 4075 (the Prophet's wounds; Fatimah washes them, Ali pours water, the ash of a burned mat)

notes: Nusaybah's account is from Ibn Ishaq via Ibn Hisham (the questioner is named there as Umm Sa'd bint Sa'd ibn al-Rabi'), not from the major hadith collections; it is framed as from 'the early biographers'. Confirm the details: the water skin, sword and bow, the shoulder wound.
Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm Bukhari 3724, 3811, 2911 and 4075.
'The rumor that he had been killed' is from the sirah (and echoed in 3:144); confirm it's acceptable without a separate citation.
'She is remembered as Umm Umarah' — confirm the kunya.
The practice mentions asking for protection in general terms, not a new prayer.

Editor: 'horsemen are coming from behind' became 'the enemy has come around it' (cavalry detail not in the cited texts); 'a younger woman' became 'another woman' (age claim); 'water at dawn, a shield at midday, ash at evening' replaced with 'a water skin, a raised hand, a shield, a handful of ash', since the sources give no such times.
Audit: Ibn Ishaq has Nusaybah carrying water to give the fighters a drink, not 'for the wounded'; hook, myth and fork made consistent. Cut the unsourced 'none of them could change the battle'.
